Part 1: The Data (2 points)¶

We will be exploring a data set on Women's March Madness (Basketball). This adapted data set contains historical records of every NCAA Division I Women’s Basketball Tournament appearance since the tournament began in 1982 up until 2018. Sourced from official NCAA, the adapted data set captures tournament results across more than four decades of collegiate women’s basketball. All data is sourced from the NCAA and contains the data behind the story The Rise and Fall Of Women’s NCAA Tournament Dynasties.

The data set can be read in from the following url: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/diverse-data-hub/diversedata/refs/heads/main/data-clean/womensmarchmadness.csv

To help you with the analysis, here is a table of descriptions of each of the variables present in the model.

Variable Description
year Year
school School Name
seed Seed. The 0 seeding designation in 1983 notes the eight teams that played an opening-round game to become the No. 8 seed in each region.
conference Conference
conf_wins Conference Wins
conf_losses Conference Losses
conf_wins_pct Conference Win Percentage
conf_rank Place in Conference
division Conference Division
reg_wins Regional Wins
reg_losses Regional Losses
reg_wins_pct Regional Win Percentage
bid Whether the school qualified with an automatic bid (by winning its conference or conference tournament) or an at-large bid. [‘at-large’, ‘auto’]
first_game_at_home Whether the school played its first-round tournament games on its home court. [‘Y’, ‘N’]
tourney_wins Tourney Wins
tourney_losses Tourney Losses
tourney_finish Ordered categories: [‘opening_round_loss’ < ‘first_round_loss’ < ‘second_round_loss’ < ‘top_16_loss’ < ‘top_8_loss’ < ‘top_4_loss’ < ‘top_2_loss’ < ‘champ’]
total_wins Total Wins
total_losses Total Losses
total_wins_pct Total Win Percentage

Part 5: Analysis (34 points)¶

In this section, you will describe your data analysis and perform it.

Task 5.1 Plan out your analysis (10 points)¶

Propose a method that was covered in class that would be appropriate to use to answer your research question. You only need to build one model with one set of predictors in this section. Write a paragraph that explains the choice of method, and be sure to answer the following questions:

  • What method do you plan to use?
  • Why is this method appropriate?
  • What are the potential limitations or weaknesses of the method selected?
  • How are you going to process the data to apply the model? For example: Are you splitting the data? How? How many splits? What proportions will you use for the splits? At what stage will you split? Will there be a validation set? Will you use cross validation?
  • How will you assess the performance of the model? Explain why the performance metric(s) chosen ise appropriate.

You answer should be around 250 words or less.

I plan to use K-nearest neighbors (KNN) classification to predict if a team will win at least one game in the tournament. I will use the team's seed and regular season win percentage to make predictions. I chose KNN classification because the result has two categories: Yes and No. KNN uses similar teams to predict the result of a new team. One problem with KNN is that the result can change depending on the number of neighbors. It is also affected by the scale of the variables. I plan to split the data into 75% training data and 25% testing data. I will use the training data to build the model and use 5-fold cross-validation to find the best number of neighbors. I will also scale the predictors so they can be compared fairly. Finally, I will use the testing data to check how well the model works. I will use accuracy and a confusion matrix to see how many predictions are correct and which mistakes the model makes.

Task 5.2 Perform the Analysis (20 points)¶

  • Perform the proposed analysis.
  • Be sure to comment your code throughout so that it is easy to follow.

You may add more code cells if needed.

In [11]:
library(tidymodels)
# Remove missing values
model_data <- march_tidy |>drop_na()
# Split data into training and testing sets
set.seed(1234)
march_split <- initial_split(model_data,prop = 0.75,strata = won_game)
march_training <- training(march_split)
march_testing <- testing(march_split)
# Create a recipe and scale the predictors
march_recipe <- recipe(won_game ~ seed + reg_wins_pct,data = march_training) |>step_normalize(all_predictors())
# Create a KNN classification model
knn_spec <- nearest_neighbor(weight_func = "rectangular",neighbors = tune()) |>set_engine("kknn") |>set_mode("classification")
# Create 5-fold cross-validation
set.seed(1234)
march_vfold <- vfold_cv(march_training,v = 5,strata = won_game)
# Create workflow
march_workflow <- workflow() |>add_recipe(march_recipe) |>add_model(knn_spec)
# Test different K values
set.seed(1234)
march_results <- march_workflow |>tune_grid(resamples = march_vfold,grid = tibble(neighbors = seq(1, 31, by = 2)),metrics = metric_set(accuracy))
# Find the best K value
best_k <- march_results |>select_best(metric = "accuracy")
best_k
# Build the final model
march_final_workflow <- march_workflow |>finalize_workflow(best_k)
# Train the model
march_final_fit <- march_final_workflow |>fit(data = march_training)
# Make predictions using testing data
march_predictions <- march_final_fit |>predict(march_testing) |>bind_cols(march_testing)
# Check model accuracy
march_accuracy <- march_predictions |>metrics(truth = won_game,estimate = .pred_class)
march_accuracy
# Create a confusion matrix
march_confusion <- march_predictions |>conf_mat(truth = won_game,estimate = .pred_class)
march_confusion

Part 6: Discuss your Results (10 points)¶

In this section, you will discuss some interesting findings from your analysis in Part 5

Task 6.1: Discuss your findings (10 points)¶

In 1 to 2 paragraphs (approx. 300 words or less):

  • Summarize what you found from the analysis in Part 5, in relation to your research question of interest.
  • The data science workflow is an iterative process. Discuss if at any point you had to adjust your analysis plan based on the results.
  • Discuss whether this is what you expected, or if anything was surprising.
  • Discuss the impact of the results, and what future questions this could lead to.

Our goal was to predict if a team could win at least one game in the NCAA Women's Basketball Tournament using its seed and regular season win percentage. We used a KNN classification model and found that the best number of neighbors was 13. The accuracy of our model was about 72.22%. The model correctly predicted 205 teams that won at least one game and 172 teams that did not win a game. However, it also made 145 incorrect predictions. This shows that our model can make useful predictions, but it is not always correct.

During the analysis, we tested different numbers of neighbors using cross-validation and chose the best one. I expected the seed and regular season win percentage to help predict tournament results, so the result was not very surprising. However, I think the model could still be improved. Basketball games can be affected by many things, such as injuries and team performance on the day of the game. In the future, we could use more information, such as team statistics and past tournament results, to see if we can make better predictions.
